summary: The first specification of the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, a framework for giving configuration information to hosts on a TCP/IP network. It was replaced by RFC 1541.

eli5.summary: When you arrive at a hotel, the front desk hands you a room key and tells you where things are. DHCP does that for a computer joining a network.

questions: how do you renew a dhcp lease
subtitle: Automatic assignment of network configuration to Internet hosts.

tldr.problem: When a new computer joins a network, someone must manually configure its IP address and other parameters. This is error-prone and does not scale for networks with many devices.
tldr.mechanism: DHCP is a client-server protocol where a DHCP server holds a pool of IP addresses and configuration options. When a client boots and broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER message, the server offers an address and settings; the client selects one and requests it with DHCPREQUEST; the server confirms with DHCPACK. Leases expire, allowing address reuse.
tldr.outcome: Computers can now join networks and configure themselves automatically. DHCP enabled large networks of mobile and temporary devices. It was superseded by RFC 1541.

facts.label: DHCP message types
facts.value: 7 (DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, DECLINE, ACK, NAK, RELEASE)

today: RFC 1531 is a Proposed Standard that was superseded by RFC 1541, which corrected some ambiguities. DHCP remains the standard mechanism for automatic IP configuration on the Internet. Modern DHCP implementations adhere to RFC 1541 or later standards, and DHCP is in use on virtually every network from home routers to large enterprises. IPv6 has DHCP for IPv6 (DHCPv6) for similar purposes.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Setting up a computer to work on a network requires configuration of many parameters: an IP address, a subnet mask, a default gateway, DNS servers, and other options. In the early Internet, a network administrator had to manually enter these values on each device, which was slow, error-prone, and did not scale.

DHCP solves this by providing a mechanism for automatic allocation of an IP address to a host, dynamic allocation of an address for a limited lease period (allowing reuse), and manual allocation (the server delivers an address that the administrator assigned). A DHCP client broadcasts a request on its local network, a server responds with available configuration, and the client accepts it. Most importantly, addresses are automatically reclaimed when no longer in use, so a pool of addresses can serve more hosts than if each had a permanent assignment.
sections.eli5: Instead of making each computer remember lots of numbers, a server keeps them and hands them out as needed. When a computer leaves, the server gets the address back and gives it to the next computer.

sections.title: DHCP Messages and the Lease Lifecycle
sections.content:
DHCP defines seven message types, each carrying specific information. A DHCPDISCOVER message is broadcast by a newly booting client to locate any available DHCP server. Each server that can serve the client responds with a DHCPOFFER, which proposes a configuration including an IP address (in the 'yiaddr' field) and a lease duration.

The client then broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST, naming the server it selected. This tells that server to commit the address to persistent storage and tells other servers their offers were declined. The selected server responds with DHCPACK, confirming the configuration. If the request cannot be satisfied (for example, because the offered address was allocated to another client), the server sends DHCPNAK. If the client detects a problem with the configuration, it sends DHCPDECLINE and restarts. When done, the client can send DHCPRELEASE to give back the address early.

The lease has a duration; the client SHOULD request renewal before it expires and MUST stop using the address if the lease expires without renewal.
sections.eli5: The client shouts 'I need a configuration!', servers answer 'I have one!', the client picks the best and says 'I want yours!', the chosen server says 'OK, it is yours for X hours', and when the time is up, the client can ask for more time or give it back.

sections.title: Message Format and BOOTP Compatibility
sections.content:
DHCP messages use the BOOTP message format from RFC 951, which begins with an 'op' field (1 for BOOTREQUEST from client, 2 for BOOTREPLY from server), hardware type, hardware address length, and hops count (for relay agents). A transaction ID ('xid') uniquely identifies a client-server conversation. The 'ciaddr' field holds the client's current IP address (zero if the client has none), 'yiaddr' holds the server's offer or assignment, and 'giaddr' holds a relay agent address if the message crossed a router.

The 'options' field (at least 312 octets) contains tagged parameters. Every DHCP message includes a DHCP message type option. Other options define the server identifier, lease time, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, and many other parameters. Compatibility with BOOTP clients is maintained: a DHCP server can serve BOOTP clients, and BOOTP relay agents can forward DHCP messages.
sections.eli5: The message is like a standard form with blanks for the client's address, the offered address, relay agent address, and a section for additional options. Every DHCP message says what type it is (DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, etc.).

sections.title: The Configuration Process: Initial Lease and Renewal
sections.content:
When a client starts, it enters the INIT state and broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER. The client MAY suggest values for the address and lease time in its options. BOOTP relay agents on other subnets forward the broadcast to DHCP servers not on the client's local segment.

Upon receiving one or more DHCPOFFER messages, the client selects one server's offer (typically the first received, or based on offered parameters). It broadcasts DHCPREQUEST, including the 'server identifier' option to name its choice. The server commits the address to storage and returns DHCPACK with the lease duration.

If the client has a previously assigned address (e.g., from a reboot), it can skip DISCOVER and OFFER and send DHCPREQUEST directly, including the old address in the 'ciaddr' field. If the server recognizes the lease, it replies with DHCPACK. If not (for example, the client has moved to a new subnet), the server responds with DHCPNAK, forcing the client to request a new address via the full process.

At lease expiration, the client broadcasts DHCPREQUEST to renew. If the server agrees, it returns DHCPACK with a new lease period. If the server does not respond, the client waits until 87.5% of the lease has passed before giving up and entering INIT state to request a new address.
sections.eli5: When a computer boots, it asks 'Anyone have a configuration?' and servers answer. The computer picks one and confirms its choice. If the computer has had an address before, it can ask 'Is my old address still valid?' If not, it goes through the full asking process. When time is up, the computer can ask for more time or get a new address.

sections.title: Design Goals and Configuration Options
sections.content:
DHCP was designed as a mechanism, not a policy: administrators can define local policies for address allocation (e.g., 'reserve certain addresses for servers'). Hosts require no manual configuration; DHCP eliminates hand entry of parameters. The protocol does not require a server on every subnet; BOOTP/DHCP relay agents forward requests across routers. Multiple overlapping DHCP servers can be deployed for reliability and load distribution.

DHCP defines many configuration options, including the subnet mask, routers, domain name servers, NTP servers, print servers, and vendor-specific information. A client can request specific options via the 'parameter request list' option. The RFC notes that DHCP does not address host registration in the Domain Name System (DNS) and is not suitable for configuring routers, which require administrative oversight.
sections.eli5: The design lets network managers set their own rules for handing out addresses. It works across routers, allows multiple backup servers, and can deliver lots of different configuration options depending on what the client asks for.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Alternatives
sections.content:
DHCP must coexist with statically configured hosts and with other network protocols. The RFC also surveys prior work: RARP (Reverse Address Resolution Protocol) addressed address discovery but not general configuration; BOOTP provided a bootstrap mechanism but lacked dynamic allocation; TFTP provided boot file transport; and Sun's bootparams offered configuration but was proprietary.

DHCP captures the relay agent behavior from BOOTP and is interoperable with BOOTP clients and relay agents, making migration straightforward. A network can run both DHCP and BOOTP simultaneously, and a DHCP server can serve both DHCP and BOOTP clients. This compatibility was essential for gradual adoption across diverse networks.
sections.eli5: DHCP works alongside the old ways of setting up computers so networks can transition gradually. It is compatible with earlier protocols like BOOTP, so old equipment and new equipment can coexist.
